name: Caching
intent: Keep copies of frequently used data in a fast place so most requests never reach the slow source.
scenario: A product page reads from a database. The same few popular products are requested thousands of times, and each read costs a slow database query.
problem: Reading from the database or computing a result is slow and expensive, and the database has a limited number of requests it can serve per second. If most traffic asks for the same few items, repeating that work every time wastes time and can overload the database long before the site is truly busy.

howItWorks.title: Check the cache first (cache-aside)
howItWorks.text: The application asks the cache for the key. A hit returns the stored value in microseconds. A miss falls through to the database, and the result is stored in the cache for next time.

howItWorks.title: Eviction when the cache is full
howItWorks.text: Memory is limited, so something must go. LRU drops the item unused for longest. LFU drops the least frequently used. FIFO drops the oldest. The best policy depends on how the traffic repeats.

howItWorks.title: Expiry and invalidation
howItWorks.text: A cached copy can go stale when the source changes. A TTL (time to live) bounds how stale it can get. Explicit invalidation deletes or updates the entry when the data is written. Both are needed in practice.

howItWorks.title: Write strategies
howItWorks.text: Write-through updates the cache and database together, so reads stay fresh at the cost of slower writes. Write-back updates the cache first and the database later, which is fast but can lose data. Write-around skips the cache on writes and lets reads refill it.

howItWorks.title: Caches exist at every layer
howItWorks.text: Browser, CDN, application memory, a shared cache like Redis, and the database's own buffers. Each layer cuts load on the one behind it, and each can serve stale data.

pros: Much lower latency for repeated reads
Protects the database from repeated identical work
Cheap way to raise throughput without new servers
Can keep serving something while the source is slow or down
cons: Stale data: the cache and the source can disagree
Invalidation is famously hard to get right
Extra moving part to size, monitor and keep available
A cold cache (after a restart) sends a burst of traffic to the database
whenToUse: A small set of items accounts for most of the traffic
The result is expensive to compute or fetch
whenNotToUse: Data changes constantly and must always be exact (balances, inventory at checkout)
Almost every request asks for something different, so hit rate stays low
The source is already fast and lightly loaded
pitfalls: Cache stampede: a popular key expires and hundreds of requests all hit the database at once
Caching errors or empty results by mistake and serving them for the whole TTL
Unbounded keys (for example one key per search string) filling the cache with items that are never reused
Relying on the cache for correctness: it can be emptied at any time

roles.label: Application
roles.description: Asks the cache first, then the database.

quiz.question: A site serves 10,000 reads per second from a cache with a 90% hit rate, and its database can handle 2,000 reads per second. A new filter feature makes most queries unique and the hit rate falls to 70%. What happens?
options: The database receives about 1,000 reads per second, as before, because the cache still takes most of the traffic.
The database receives about 7,000 reads per second, because misses are the 70% share of traffic.
The database load stays the same, because the cache is only a latency tool and not a load tool.
The database receives about 3,000 reads per second, above its limit, so it slows down or fails.
quiz.explanation: Misses are 30% of 10,000, which is 3,000 per second. A small drop in hit rate can triple the database load, so hit rate is a capacity number and not just a speed number.

quiz.question: A profile service uses a write-back cache so that updates return in 1 ms. The cache flushes to the database every 2 seconds. The cache node crashes. What is the risk?
options: Reads return stale data after the restart, but all acknowledged updates are safe in the database.
Updates acknowledged in the last 2 seconds may be lost, as they were only in the cache.
The database is overloaded by a flood of flushes, but the data is complete and correct.
Nothing is lost, because the cache writes to the database before it answers the client.
quiz.explanation: Write-back trades durability for speed: the database lags behind. Write-through would keep them in step at the cost of slower writes.

quiz.question: A home-page entry is read 5,000 times a second, has a TTL of 60 seconds and takes 3 seconds to rebuild from the database. Every minute the database spikes at the moment it expires. What is the best fix?
options: Increase the TTL to 10 minutes, so the expiry and the spike happen ten times less often.
Switch the eviction policy from LRU to LFU, so a popular key is never chosen for removal.
Let one request rebuild the value while the others wait or get the old copy, and add jitter to the TTL.
Give the cache more memory, so the entry is not evicted before its TTL runs out.
quiz.explanation: This is a stampede: thousands of requests miss together and all rebuild the same value. A longer TTL only makes the spike rarer, and eviction policy is not the cause since the key expires by TTL.
